title: Cc No. 365/12 vs Rekha on 23 August, 2012
full_text: Cc No. 365/12 vs Rekha on 23 August, 2012 IN THE COURT OF SH. VIKRANT VAID, MM(NI ACT­02)/ SOUTH, SAKET COURTS, NEW DELHI Unique Id No. 02403R0972472003 CC No. 365/12 Prem Chand @ Prem Chander, S/o Sh. Sumari Lal, R/o D­1877, Uday Chand Marg, Kotla Mubarakpur, New Delhi. .......................Complainant Versus Rekha W/o Sh. Kalicharan, Flat no. 28, Pocket­D, Mayur Vihar, Phase­III, Delhi. .............................. Accused OFFENCE COMPLAINED OF OR PROVED : Section 138 of Negotiable Instrument Act. PLEA OF ACCUSED : Pleaded not guilty DATE OF INSTITUTION : 24.09.2004 DATE OF RESERVING ORDER : 23.08.2012 FINAL ORDER : Acquittal DATE OF PRONOUNCEMENT : 23.08.2012 Prem Chand @ Prem Chander Vs Rekha CC No. 365/12 Page No. 1 of 17 JUDGMENT 1. The present complaint is filed by Prem Chand against Rekha under Section 138 of Negotiable Instrument Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as " The Act "). 2. It is the case of the complainant that he advanced a friendly loan of Rs. 70,000/­ to the accused on her request. In discharge of legal liability, the accused issued two cheques of Rs. 20,000/­ and Rs. 50,000/­. The present complaint is in respect of cheque of Rs. 50,000/­ The complainant presented the said cheque for payment but the the same were dishonoured with remarks 'Insufficient funds'. A legal demand notice was served upon the accused by complainant. Despite service of legal notice, the accused failed to make the payment of cheque amount within the stipulated period. Against the factual matrix, complainant instituted the present complaint against the accused. 3. The predecessor of this court took cognizance of the offence under Section 138 of The Act and summoned the accused. Prem Chand @ Prem Chander Vs Rekha CC No. 365/12 Page No. 2 of 17 4. Accused appeared pursuant to the process issued by the Court. Notice under Section 251 CrPC was read and explained to the accused to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. Consequently, the case was listed for post notice complainant evidence. 5. Complainant in his evidence examined himself as sole witness CW1. He substantiated the averments made in the complaint in his examination in chief. He proved the following documents :­ i. The cheque bearing no. 049736 dated 25.04.2012 as Ex CW­1/A. ii. Pay­in­slip dated 10.08.2004 as Ex CW­1/B. iii. Cheque return memo dated 13.08.2004 pertaining to Ex.CW1/A as Ex CW1/C. iv. Legal notice dated 18.08.2004 and postal receipt as Ex CW1/D. Vide separate statement, complainant's evidence was closed and matter was listed for examination of accused under Section 313 Cr.P.C. 6. All incriminating circumstances were put to the accused. Accused denied the averments made in the complaint and stated that the cheque in question was given as a security against loan of Prem Chand @ Prem Chander Vs Rekha CC No. 365/12 Page No. 3 of 17 Rs.20,000/­ obtained by her husband. 7. In defence evidence, accused examined two witnesses. Mr. Kalicharan, husband of the accused was examined as DW­1. He deposed that he had obtained friendly loan of Rs. 20,000/­ from the complainant against which the cheque in question was issued in blank as a security. He further deposed that the complainant did not return the cheque and misused the same. Accused herself appeared as DW­2 and deposed on the same lines as DW­1. Vide separate statement, defence evidence was closed and matter was listed for final arguments. 8. I have heard the final arguments advanced by the rival counsels and perused the record carefully. 9. The essential ingredients which need be proved for constituting the offence under Section 138 of The Act were discussed in the case Jugesh Sehgal Vs. Shamsher Singh Gogi 2009 (9) SCALE 455. The relevant portion of the said judgment reads as under: "9. It is manifest that to constitute an offence under Section Prem Chand @ Prem Chander Vs Rekha CC No. 365/12 Page No. 4 of 17 138 of The Act , the following ingredients are required to be fulfilled: (i) a person must have drawn a cheque on an account maintained by him in a bank for payment of a certain amount of money to another person from out of that account; (ii) The cheque should have been issued for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability; (iii) that cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity whichever is earlier; (iv) that cheque is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of the account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with the bank; (v) the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within 15 days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid; (vi) the drawer of such cheque fails to make payment of the said amount of money to the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque within 15 days of the receipt of the said notice. 10. Let us now examine whether the complainant has proved the Prem Chand @ Prem Chander Vs Rekha CC No. 365/12 Page No. 5 of 17 necessary ingredients of the offence under Section 138 of The Act or not. The first ingredient of the offence stands proved as original cheque is placed on record as Ex. CW1/A and the issuance of same is admitted by the accused. The second ingredient of the offence is that the cheque must have been issued in discharge of legal liability. As the signatures on the cheque are admitted, the presumptions raised under Section 139 of The Act become applicable and the issuance of cheque in discharge of the legal liabilty stands proved. The law on this point has been succinctly laid down by the Hon'ble Apex Court in Rangappa v. Sri Mohan AIR 2010 SC 1898. The third ingredient of the offence is that cheque must presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date mentioned on it. The cheque Ex.CW1/A was returned back unpaid on 13.08.2004 . The cheque is dated 25.04.2004 so it is evident that it was presented for payment within the statutory period of six months. The fourth ingredient of the offence if that the cheque( s) Prem Chand @ Prem Chander Vs Rekha CC No. 365/12 Page No. 6 of 17 must be returned unpaid. The cheque was returned unpaid for the reason 'Funds insufficient'. The original bank return­memo Ex.CW1/C placed on record proves dishonour of cheque by virtue of presumption raised under Section 146 of The Act and during the trial, Ex.CW1/C went uncontroverted. The fifth ingredient of the offence is that the demand notice must be issued to the accused within 30 days of the intimation of dishonour of cheque and same be served upon the accused. The RL­AD receipts Ex CW1/D showing dispatch of legal notice has been placed on record by the complainant. Accused has not disputed the address mentioned in the legal notice and the postal receipts. In C.C.Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed and Anr 2007(7) SCALE 380, the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that in case the legal notice is sent at the correct address by registered post, there is sufficient compliance of the provisions of Sections 138(c) of The Act. In the light of law enunciated in the foregoing judgment and material on record, the service of legal notice stands duly proved. The last ingredient is that the accused must not have made Prem Chand @ Prem Chander Vs Rekha CC No. 365/12 Page No. 7 of 17 the payment of the cheque amount within fifteen days of the receipt of legal notice. Non payment of cheque amount is a negative fact which is also not controverted by the accused. As such non­payment of the cheque amount stands established. All the necessary ingredients for the offence have been made out against the accused with the aid and assistance of the presumptions raised under The Act . So the complainant has discharged the initial burden of proving his case beyond reasonable doubt and now the onus shifted upon the accused to come up with a probable defence and rebut the presumptions raised against him and put the burden back on the complainant. 11. The plea of defence of the accused is three­fold. Firstly, she never obtained any friendly loan from the complainant. Infact her husband had obtained a loan of Rs.20,000/­ from the complainant. Secondly, the cheque was issued as a security for the loan obtained by her husband and not in discharge of any legal liability. Lastly, the debt is not legally recoverable and therefore the provisions of Section 138 of The Act are not attracted. Prem Chand @ Prem Chander Vs Rekha CC No. 365/12 Page No. 8 of 17 Accused has maintained a consistent stand that she did not obtain any loan from the complainant and the cheque Ex.CW1/A was issued as a security. No inconsistency whatsoever has crept in her stand at any stage. 12. I shall first deal with the defence plea that the complaint is not maintainable as the alleged debt is not legally recoverable. As per complainant, the loan transaction in question is a cash transaction. Complainant admitted in his testimony that he did not disclose the alleged transaction before the Income Tax authorities. He expressed his inability to provide any evidence regarding the alleged savings of Rs. 70,000/­ lying with him in cash at relevant point of time. The complainant has not satisfactorily established the source of amount advanced. It makes it evident that the transaction was with respect to unaccounted money. It was bounden duty of the complainant to disclose the transaction in his Income Tax Returns. 13. Section 269SS of the Income Tax Act lays down that the loan above Rs.20,000/­ shall be payable or received by account Prem Chand @ Prem Chander Vs Rekha CC No. 365/12 Page No. 9 of 17 payee cheque or demand draft. Contravention of Section 269SS renders the transaction unlawful and attracts penalty under Section 271D of the Income Tax Act. The object of section 138 of the said Act was to ensure that commercial and mercantile activities are conducted in smooth and healthy manner. The explanation to Section 138 of The Act clearly provides that a debt or other liability referred to in section means a legally enforceable debt or other liability. The alleged liability to repay the loan(not disclosed in the Income Tax Return) cannot be a legally recoverable liability. If such liability is held to be a legally recoverable debt, it will render the explanation to section 138 of the said Act nugatory. It will defeat the very object of Section 138 of The Act of ensuring that the commercial and mercantile activities are conducted in a healthy manner. The provision of Section 138 cannot be resorted to for recovery of an unaccounted amount. A cheque issued in discharge of alleged liability of repaying "unaccounted and undislcosed" cash amount cannot be said to be a cheque issued in discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability within the meaning of explanation of section 138 of the said Act. The Prem Chand @ Prem Chander Vs Rekha CC No. 365/12 Page No. 10 of 17 transaction is unlawful under the Income tax laws. Court cannot be permitted to be used as a tool to recover such "unaccounted and undislcosed" money. Such an effort to misuse the provision of section 138 of The Act has to be discouraged. The loan in question is not a legally recoverable debt and therefore offence under section 138 of The Act is not made out. I am fortified in my view by the judgment of Hon'ble Bombay High Court in Sanjay Mishra vs Ms.Kanishka Kapoor @ Nikki 2009 MLR 155 which also makes it clear that such an undisclosed loan transaction does not fall in the category of a legally recoverable debt. Therefore, even if the entire prosecution story is found reliable yet the offence under Section 138 of The Act is not made out as the debt/loan is not legally recoverable. 14. It is averred in the legal notice and complaint that it is husband of the accused who is a friend of the complainant. Deviating from the same, CW1 deposed in affidavit of evidence that accused is his friend. Further, complainant's averment of friendly loan is absolutely bald and uncorroborated by any Prem Chand @ Prem Chander Vs Rekha CC No. 365/12 Page No. 11 of 17 documentary or ocular evidence. Conspicuously, the complaint is devoid of details as to the date, place, time, duration, interest or witnesses to the loan transaction. Even the mode of payment( viz. cash, cheque, transfer etc) has also not been mentioned in the complaint. 15. In complaint and legal notice Ex.CW1/D, it is averred that Rs.70,000/­ was advanced as loan to the accused. In stark contradiction, in the affidavits of evidence(both at pre­summoning and post notice stage), CW1 deposed that a sum of Rs.50,000/­ only was advanced to the accused. The contradiction remained unexplained throughout. 16. There are contradictions regarding the amount which was allegedly advanced in instalments. CW1 testified in cross­ examination dated 28.07.2008 that he had advanced Rs. 70,0000/­ to the accused in two instalments of Rs.20,000/­ and Rs. 50,000/­. It is pertinent that as per legal notice notice Ex.CW1/D, the loan was advanced in two instalments of Rs.35,000/­ each. Once again, there is apparent irreconcilable contradiction in the complainant's story. Prem Chand @ Prem Chander Vs Rekha CC No. 365/12 Page No. 12 of 17 17. Later, CW1 expressed his inability to state whether the loan was advanced in a single or multiple instalment(s). The relevant portion of his testimony dated 18.08.2012 reads as: "...I cannot say whether the payment was made by me to the accused in single or multiple instalments..." The aforesaid testimony exposes the falsehood of the complainant's cased. CW1 has not only made contradictory statements regarding the amount of loan advanced in toto & in instalments, but also made repugnant utterances as to the number of instalments in which loan was advanced. The contradictory statements of the complainant as to the amount of the loan advanced in toto & in instalments, number of instalments in which loan was advanced and relation with the accused shake the very foundation of his case. Prosecution has miserably failed to stand on its own legs. There is no doubt in my mind that the complainant's story is absolutely incredible, false and ill­conceived. Prem Chand @ Prem Chander Vs Rekha CC No. 365/12 Page No. 13 of 17 18. Further, in his testimony dated 18.08.2012, CW1 asserted that the signature and the particulars of the cheque were filled by the accused in his presence. However, he subsequently admitted that the particulars of the cheque were filled in different inks and different handwriting. His admission as to different handwriting falsifies his assertion that the particulars of cheque were filled by accused. Infact, the use of two different inks indicates that the particulars and signatures were put at different times. The testimony of defence witnesses is categorical that the cheque in question was issued in blank as security which was later misused by complainant after filing it. These circumstances further demolish the complainant's case and point towards the genuineness of defence plea . 19. The credibility of a witness is judged from the inherent probabilities of truthfulness of his testimony and him withstanding the test of cross­examination. Cross­examination is the touchstone of the truthfulness and veracity of the statements made in the examination­in­chief. Being the solitary prosecution witness, complainant's(CW1) cross­examination acquires significance and Prem Chand @ Prem Chander Vs Rekha CC No. 365/12 Page No. 14 of 17 requires greater scrutiny. Complainant was grilled at length by the counsel for the accused. As discussed above, his testimony was found to be full of inconsistencies and contradictions on material aspects. Hence it shall be unsafe to base conviction of the accused on such weak testimony which is absolutely uncorroborated. 20. In the recent judgment of its Full Bench in Rangappa v. Sri Mohan AIR 2010 SC 1898, the Hon'ble Supreme Court dealt elaborately with the issue of rebuttal of presumptions envisaged in the Act and observed(relevant portion is reproduced): "..... In the absence of compelling justifications, reverse onus clauses usually impose an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. Keeping this in view, it is a settled position that when an accused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139 , the standard of proof for doing so is that of `preponderance of probabilities'. Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the prosecution can fail" . 21. As quoted above, the standard of proof so as to prove a Prem Chand @ Prem Chander Vs Rekha CC No. 365/12 Page No. 15 of 17 defence on the part of an accused is 'preponderance of probabilities'. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which he relies. After carefully scrutinizing and analyzing the evidence together with the circumstances discussed above, I am of the opinion that there is sufficient material on record to displace the presumptions raised under The Act . The material on record is more consistent with the innocence of the accused than her guilt. Moreover, the debt is not legally recoverable(already discussed). There is no doubt in my mind that the accused has come up with a highly probable defence to successfully throw out the presumptions raised against him. 22. In totality of the circumstances and the discussions above, I am of the considered opinion that the accused has proved her defence not only on the basis of preponderance of probabilities but also on the technical ground that the debt is not legally recoverable. She has successfully rebutted the presumptions raised under the Act. On the other hand, complainant has failed to prove Prem Chand @ Prem Chander Vs Rekha CC No. 365/12 Page No. 16 of 17 his case beyond reasonable doubt against the accused. Accordingly, the accused is acquitted. Announced in the open Court (Vikrant Vaid) on 23.08.2012 MM(NIAct)­02/South Saket/Delhi Prem Chand @ Prem Chander Vs Rekha CC No. 365/12 Page No. 17 of 17
